frase_gancho.texto: Clay women with festive hairstyles and hips of fertile earth.

puente_narrativo.texto: Among the figurines, one seems to move. Look for the dancer with rattles on her legs: the village did not only work and bury its dead, it also celebrated.

guion_corto.texto: These are the “Pretty Ladies” of Tlatilco, a name given to them by the artist Miguel Covarrubias in the last century. They are handmade clay figurines, between ten and fifteen centimeters tall, with a narrow waist, wide hips and thick thighs, and feet that are barely suggested. What is carefully made is everything else: braided hairstyles, headdresses, ear ornaments, necklaces, and red or yellow paint. They were found in houses and in tombs, and they are linked to fertility, the earth and the harvests. Notice the variety: each one has a different hairstyle, as if they were portraits. They are also among the earliest examples of fashion in Mesoamerica.

guion_largo.texto:
They were named by Miguel Covarrubias, an artist famous for his caricatures who became an archaeologist out of passion and was among the first to understand what was coming out of the brickyards of Tlatilco. In Spanish they are known as “Mujeres Bonitas,” which means “Pretty Ladies,” for the same reason: they proved irresistible. Thousands have been found, and the best way to understand why is to look at how much care whoever modeled them put into them.

Notice the body first: a narrow waist, very wide hips and thighs, and feet barely hinted at with a pair of cuts. It is an exaggerated form, on purpose. What truly interested their makers was higher up: hairstyles with crossed braids, headdresses, caps, round ear ornaments, necklaces, and red and yellow paint on the face and body. Some even wear small ornaments of pyrite, a mineral that shines like a mirror.

Now notice how they were made. They were modeled by hand, from clay paste, and the ornaments were added with small strips and little balls of clay stuck on, a technique called pastillaje. The eyes, the mouth and the designs of the hairstyle were marked with pointed tools, and at the end they were painted red, from hematite, and yellow. A meticulous job, repeated thousands of times, which speaks of workshops and of skilled women artisans.

They are not all alike. Some carry a child, others hold an animal, others seem to dance. Who were they? Perhaps portraits of women of the village, perhaps offerings to ask for children and good harvests, perhaps household amulets. No one knows for certain, and that doubt is part of their charm. At many Preclassic sites, moreover, figurines have been found that were broken on purpose, perhaps as part of a ritual; others, intact, accompanying the deceased.

What does seem clear is the underlying idea. For farming peoples, woman and earth had a similar destiny: both give life, and both need care. That association survived the centuries. In the Teotihuacán Hall you will find [Chalchiuhtlicue](mna_s04_chalchiuhtlicue), goddess of flowing water and of fertility; in the Mexica Hall, [Coatlicue](mna_s06_coatlicue), the Earth Mother who gives and who claims. These figurines are the first sketches of that lineage of goddesses.

There is another reason to linger a while. Covarrubias was also one of the defenders of an idea that you will see in the Gulf Coast Hall: that the Olmec were the “mother culture” of Mesoamerica. In Tlatilco, figurines with Olmec features appeared, and that is why these pieces mattered so much: they were a window onto how a village of the highlands looked out toward a larger world.

And one last curiosity, this time about fashion. Upstairs, in the ethnography halls, you will see how the custom of adorning the head, the ears and the neck is still alive in huipiles, rebozos and headdresses of today. Whoever styled the hair of these clay women three thousand years ago would have understood perfectly someone getting ready for the town festival.

texto.pregunta: Myth: The “Pretty Ladies” are goddesses who were worshipped in a temple.
texto.respuesta: Reality: They were household and funerary objects; their exact meaning is still debated, but they are linked to fertility, the earth and life in the village.
